test.title: Emotional intelligence (EQ)
test.about:
Emotional intelligence is the ability to notice, understand and manage emotions, both your own and other people's. It matters for relationships, work and well-being.

Short form: the Wong and Law Emotional Intelligence Scale (WLEIS, 16 questions), which scores four abilities: understanding your own emotions, understanding others' emotions, using emotions to motivate yourself and regulating your emotions.
Long form: the WLEIS plus the Schutte Self-Report Emotional Intelligence Test (33 questions), for a second, broader measurement.
test.instructions: You will see {n} statements about emotions. For each one, choose how much you agree that it describes you as you generally are. There are no right or wrong answers.
test.chart_subtitle: Your average answer on each part, shown as a share of the scale. Higher means a stronger ability, as you see yourself.
test.agree: Both questionnaires give a similar picture.
test.disagree: The two questionnaires give somewhat different pictures, which can happen because they ask about emotions in different ways.
test.note: These scores compare your answers with the scale itself, not with other people, because published norms differ between countries. Self-reports show how you see yourself; others may see you differently.

SEA.name: Understanding your own emotions
SEA.about: Noticing what you feel and knowing why.
SEA.high: You are well aware of your feelings and usually know why you feel the way you do. This helps you make choices that fit what you really need.
SEA.average: You often know what you feel and why, though some feelings can be hard to name, especially under stress.
SEA.low: Your feelings can be hard to read or name. This is a skill that can be learned.
SEA.tip: Pause a few times a day and name what you feel in one word. A short evening journal also helps you see patterns.

OEA.name: Understanding others' emotions
OEA.about: Reading other people's feelings from what they say and do.
OEA.high: You read people well and pick up on their feelings from small signals. Others probably find you understanding and sensitive.
OEA.average: You usually notice how others feel, though you may miss quieter signals.
OEA.low: Other people's feelings can be hard for you to read, which can lead to misunderstandings.
OEA.tip: In conversations, watch faces and tone, and check your guess: "You seem a bit tired, is that right?"

UOE.name: Using emotions to motivate yourself
UOE.about: Setting goals, encouraging yourself and keeping going.
UOE.high: You turn your feelings into drive: you set goals, encourage yourself and keep trying when things get hard.
UOE.average: You can usually motivate yourself, though your drive may dip when you feel low.
UOE.low: It can be hard to motivate yourself, especially when your mood is low.
UOE.tip: Break goals into small steps, celebrate each one, and remind yourself why the goal matters to you.

ROE.name: Regulating your emotions
ROE.about: Staying calm and recovering quickly when upset.
ROE.high: You handle strong feelings well: you can calm down, control your temper and recover quickly from setbacks.
ROE.average: You manage your feelings reasonably well, though strong emotions sometimes take over.
ROE.low: Strong feelings can be hard to control and may take a while to settle.
ROE.tip: When upset, slow your breathing (breathe out longer than in), name the feeling, and wait a moment before you react.

overall_texts.high: Overall you see yourself as emotionally skilled: you understand and handle emotions well in yourself and others.
overall_texts.average: Overall your emotional skills are in the middle of the scale: solid in some areas, with room to grow in others.
overall_texts.low: Overall you see your emotional skills as an area to develop. The good news is that emotional intelligence can be learned with practice.
